opening.headline: To automatically grade an agent's responses when there is no fixed correct answer, we explore how to design a grader and how to trust that grader.
body: An agent's responses vary each time, expressing the same meaning in different ways. It would be impossible for a human to read and evaluate hundreds of such responses daily. Therefore, an automated grading system is needed; however, if this system is poorly designed, the entire evaluation result will be incorrect.

In this class, we compare the strengths and weaknesses of three types of graders: code grading, model grading, and human grading. We then examine grade definitions that evaluate tool calling at the line level. Following this, we explore design principles such as grading rubrics, partial grading, and anti-gaming, and analyze a case where the root cause of poor results was not the agent but the grader itself.

visual.alt: A scene featuring numerous response cards accumulated over a day, with a question mark placed between them and one person reading.
labels: Who determines that someone has done well?

paragraphs: Operating an agent accumulates hundreds of responses per day. It is difficult for a human to read and evaluate all of these responses to determine whether they were handled well or not. As the number of responses increases, the reading speed becomes a bottleneck in the evaluation process.

Automatically comparing is also not easy. Responses freely formulated by users may convey the same meaning but use different sentences each time, and agents do not provide answers in a fixed format. As a result, even when the response sentences and characters exactly match the correct answer, the system may incorrectly judge it as wrong.

Ultimately, to automatically evaluate, we must delegate the question of "what constitutes a good performance" to code or a model. The entity that performs this role is the grader. If the grader is flawed, the evaluation results lose meaning. Therefore, this course focuses on how to design a grader and how to trust it.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When the evaluation score is low, how can we determine whether the cause lies in the agent or in the grader? We'll return to this topic at the end of the class.

screens.outro: First, let me recall the judgment method I am using.

screens.title: Should we decide based on code, or should we entrust it to the model?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: How are items with precisely defined strings or numbers being evaluated?
items.answer: Items with a single predefined correct answer are fastest and most reliable when compared using code. Since code always produces the same output for the same input, it consistently verifies whether strings match, tests pass, or tools are correctly invoked—ensuring that results do not change upon reevaluation.

items.prompt: How are items with multiple plausible answers being evaluated?
items.answer: Character-by-character comparison cannot distinguish between different expressions that convey the same meaning. For such items, either a model with a reference standard reads and evaluates them, or a human reads and makes the judgment. Each approach has its own advantages and disadvantages, which we compare in this course.

items.prompt: How long will it be possible for humans to read and judge in this way?
items.answer: Human judgment is the most reliable standard, but it is slow and expensive. When responses exceed hundreds per day, exhaustive review becomes impractical. Therefore, it is reasonable to use humans to review only a sample of responses or to verify the reliability of automated scoring systems.

screens.outro: I've organized my thoughts now, so let's compare the three types of graders.

screens.title: Types of grader and their respective advantages and disadvantages
screens.lead: Select each tab to explore the concepts of grader and its three features. On the last tab, you can verify methods for combining results from multiple graders.

tabs.label: What is a grader?
tabs.body: A grader is a logical mechanism that assigns a score based on one aspect of an agent's output or execution log. Multiple graders can be assigned to a single task. For example, one grader may evaluate whether the code is correct, another may assess code quality, and a third may determine whether the appropriate tools were invoked. Anthropic explains that in agent evaluation, they combine three types: code, model, and human.

tabs.label: Code grading
tabs.body: String matching (exact, regex, fuzzy), binary tests that transition from failure to pass, static analysis (linting, typing, security), result validation, tool call validation, and log analysis (number of turns completed, token usage) fall into this category. It is fast, inexpensive, objective, and produces the same output for the same input, making error detection straightforward. Its weaknesses include vulnerability to valid variations that do not exactly match the expected form and inability to handle subtle judgments.

tabs.label: Model scoring
tabs.body: Scoring based on benchmarks, natural language assertions, pairwise comparison of answers, evaluation by reference against candidate responses, and consensus among multiple models all fall within this framework. It is flexible, easily extensible, capable of capturing nuance, and supports free-form output. On the other hand, **the results are not consistently identical**, it is more expensive than code, and accuracy improvements require human judgment alignment and calibration.

tabs.label: human grading
tabs.body: Expert review, sample inspection, A/B testing, and inter-rater agreement verification fall under this category. It represents the highest quality standards and aligns with expert users' judgments. It is also used as a benchmark for adjusting model scoring. However, it is expensive and slow, and requires securing experts to scale it up.

tabs.label: Combine Results
tabs.body: There are three methods for determining the final grading score of a task. First, a weighted average of grader results is computed, and the task is passed if it exceeds a threshold. Second, a binary approach requires all graders to pass the task. Third, a hybrid method combines both approaches. Regardless of the method used, the fundamental strategy is to use multiple graders to complement each other's weaknesses.

screens.outro: Now that we know the type, let's examine the actual grader definition on a line-by-line basis.

screens.title: Read grade definition on a per-line basis
screens.lead: The following is the grader definition for evaluating tool calls. By selecting the highlighted sections, you can view the meaning of each line and the symptoms that appear when it is incorrectly used.

visual.alt: A diagram where the tool name grader and the argument grader each output either 0 or 1, and their values are summed together to produce a single result.

marks.note: A multi grader that combines multiple graders. It includes two graders, one to evaluate names and another to evaluate arguments within the listed graders, and finally combines the results into a single output. Tool calling separately evaluates names and arguments to determine which side is incorrect.

The eq operation of string_check returns 1 if two strings are exactly equal, otherwise 0. This grader is appropriate for comparing tool names, but applying the same approach in the following argument grader leads to problems.
The expected tool name. Compare it with the reference on the right to verify that the agent selected the correct tool. If a different tool was invoked, this grader returns 0.

The sample of {{ namespace.variable }} denotes a model output. output_tools refers to the list of actual tool calls made by the model, and it retrieves the function name of the first call. item refers to a row in the dataset.

It averages the results of the name grader and the argument grader, yielding 0.5 if the name is correct but the argument is wrong, and 1 if both are correct. This is an example of partial credit for a call that is only partially correct.

screens.outro: Having learned how to read definitions, I will now show the principles to uphold when designing a grader.

screens.title: Grading design principles: rubric, partial credit, bypass prevention
screens.lead: Expand each item and verify one principle at a time when designing the grader.

items.title: Order of mixing types
items.body: Whenever possible, use code graders first, add model graders where code-based evaluation is difficult, and use humans only for verification. Adopt a fast and cost-effective approach as the default, and reserve expensive methods only for absolutely necessary cases.

items.title: Dimensional KPIs
items.body: A good evaluation criteria clearly specifies what is expected at each dimension. Vague criteria lead to inconsistent judgments. It is better to have separate models of graders assess each dimension individually rather than having a single grader evaluate multiple dimensions at once.

items.title: Exit when unmounted
items.body: If a model grader makes a judgment with insufficient information, it might invent plausible values. By allowing the system to return 'Unknown' when information is lacking, such errors can be reduced.

items.title: partial grading
items.body: Tasks composed of multiple elements include partial scoring. An agent who accurately identifies the issue and confirms with the customer, but fails to process the refund, is clearly better than an agent who failed from the outset. To clearly show improvement directions, the degree of success must be represented continuously.

items.title: Bypass Prevention
items.body: Agents should not be able to easily pass evaluations through cheating. To pass, they must actually solve the problem, and the task and grader are designed so that exploiting weaknesses will not suffice.

items.title: A clear task
items.body: A good task is one where two experts independently reach the same pass/fail judgment. If the task specification is ambiguous, that ambiguity becomes noise in the evaluation score. Verify whether the task can be solved jointly using a shared reference solution.

screens.outro: Having understood the principle, let's examine an example of how a model grader corrects itself when it diverges from human judgment.

screens.title: Explanation: Bias and correction in model scoring
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Situation: Judgment diverges from human input
steps.body: The human expert reviewed the model's judgments using sample data, and in some cases, the two judgments contradict each other. This clearly reveals that the model's output is inconsistent and requires human correction.

steps.title: Step 1: Root Cause Tracing
steps.body: First, check that the benchmark is clear and unambiguous. Also, verify that a single grader is not responsible for evaluating multiple dimensions at once. If accuracy, tone, and completeness are all assessed in a single evaluation, the judgment may become biased toward one side.

steps.title: Step 2: Adjustment
steps.body: Separate graders per dimension so each only sees one dimension. Additionally, add a path that returns 'Unknown' when information is insufficient. This reduces the model's tendency to make judgments about things it does not know.

steps.title: Step 3: Calibration
steps.body: Collects instances of disagreement between human expert judgments and model judgments within the same response bundle. Identifies patterns of disagreement, for example, a tendency to rate longer answers as less appropriate, and incorporates these patterns into the benchmark. Repeats this process until disagreements are sufficiently reduced.

steps.title: Step 4: Verification
steps.body: Finally, read the record to verify that the grader is not rejecting a valid answer. Once the system is stable, human review is sometimes sufficient. However, corrections do not end with a single check; they must be re-verified whenever agents or tasks change.

screens.outro: The following example illustrates a case where the cause of low results lies on the grader side.

screens.title: Explanation: When the cause of low results was the grader rather than the agent
screens.lead: Compare the difference between attributing the same phenomenon to the agent when transitioning between two states versus attributing it to the grader.

states.label: A Case Study from the Perspective of Agents
states.body: The tool name is correct, but if arguments have the same value—such as 1 and 1.0—differing only in representation, the argument grader returns 0, and the sum result stays at 0.5. Upon observing this, one might conclude that "the agent cannot generate arguments" and begin modifying the model or prompt, leading to incorrect adjustments. In reality, the agent's invocation is valid.

states.label: Case viewed from the perspective of the grader
states.body: Reading the logs confirms that the call is valid. The root cause is the rigid configuration of the arguments grader, which compares the entire argument string using string_check and eq. The documentation explains that the grader easily downgrades subtle differences, such as expecting "1" instead of "1.0" or using abbreviated names for identifiers. The fix is to replace the arguments grader with text_similarity or score_model. Anthropic also reports a similar case: an evaluation that strictly compared the expected value "96.12" to "96.124991" saw its success rate jump from 42% to 95% after addressing issues with grading settings and ambiguous specifications. Finally, we review the logs from multiple attempts to ensure that failures are fair.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the lessons learned from the case study.

screens.title: The grader is also an evaluation target.
screens.lead: Let's revisit the initial question by reflecting on the flow of the lesson.

paragraphs: The grader consists of three types: code, model, and human, which work together to complement each other's weaknesses. Evaluation criteria are clearly defined by dimension, and partial grading and bypass prevention are designed as fundamental aspects of the assessment process.

If low results are obtained, do not solely suspect the agent—instead, review the logs to first verify whether the grader and task specifications are fair. The grader is also subject to evaluation. You cannot trust the evaluation unless you first trust the evaluation mechanism itself.

glossary.def: This is the logic for assigning a score to one aspect of agent output or execution records. Multiple scores can be assigned to a single task.
This is a code-based determination approach, such as string matching, testing, static analysis, and tool call validation. It is fast and reproducible, but vulnerable to valid variations.
This is a method where another model evaluates responses based on a benchmark. While flexible, the results are not consistently identical, requiring adjustments to align with human judgments.
This is a decision criterion specifying what is expected at each dimension. If ambiguous, the decision will be inconsistent.
This approach reflects a certain level in the result if only some of the elements are satisfied.
This defines combining the results from multiple graders into a single value using the calculate_output expression.

misconceptions.myth: The model grader is trustworthy like a human.
misconceptions.fact: Model evaluation is not consistent across runs and is more expensive than code execution. It must be calibrated against human judgment to be trustworthy.

misconceptions.myth: The code grader is the most objective, therefore always sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: Code evaluation is objective and reproducible, but it considers any valid transformation that does not exactly match the expected form as incorrect. In cases requiring subtle judgment, human or model input is necessary.

misconceptions.myth: If the result is low, it means the agent failed.
misconceptions.fact: This could be due to defects in the grader or task specifications. It is necessary to review the records to verify whether the failure is fair.

misconceptions.myth: Tool calling requires that the name and argument string be exactly the same.
misconceptions.fact: You may miss calls that have the same value but differ only in notation. Complement with similarity scoring or model scoring.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content covered in this course.
points: The grader consists of three types: code, model, and human, each complementing the others' strengths and weaknesses.
Vague criteria lead to inconsistent judgments, so they are made clearly and explicitly at each dimension.
The model grader adjusts its judgments by comparing them with human evaluations and provides the option to respond "I don't know" when uncertain.
The grader is also subject to evaluation, so its records are reviewed to verify reliability.
closing.reflectionLead: Finally, here's a question for you to think about on your own. Please feel free to recall it at your convenience—no submission or grading is required.
closing.reflection: What grounds do I have for trusting the grader I'm using, and what records could I review to verify that trust?

checks.q: In the tool calling grading settings, the "arguments" grader has "type": "string_check", "operation": "eq", yet it receives 0 points because the normal call passed 1.0 instead of argument 1. What is the appropriate action?
options: Change the model to make the factor created only as a string
Replace the grader with text_similarity or score_model.
Reduce the weight of the grader name to 0.
Remove the arguments grader and only evaluate the final answer.
checks.explain: The agent call is valid, so the issue lies in the rigid grader configuration for eq comparison. Switching to similarity or model scoring allows for tolerance of identical value notations.

wrong.0: Attributing a bug to the model when it's actually a valid call misrepresents the root cause.
wrong.2: Removing the weight of name comparison does not eliminate the rigidity of attribute comparison.
wrong.3: If you exclude factor accuracy evaluation from the assessment scope, you will fail to identify incorrect factors.
